subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If 1, ω, ω² are the cube roots of unity, then prove that (2 − ω)(2 − ω²)(2 − ω¹⁰)(2 − ω¹¹) = 49.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.73 — VSAQ chapter 13 De Moivre's Theorem, answer 119. Re-derived: ω¹⁰ = ω, ω¹¹ = ω², so the product is [(2 − ω)(2 − ω²)]² = 7² = 49; the book's answer is correct. Asked as Model Paper 3, Q3 (book p.115) and Model Paper 5, Q3 (book p.119).

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — what ω¹⁰ and ω¹¹ reduce to, and how the product is evaluated.
insider_note: Four brackets but only two different ones: ω¹⁰ = ω and ω¹¹ = ω², so the product is [(2 − ω)(2 − ω²)]². Reducing the two powers the other way round still ends at 49, so the first mark is for the reduction itself, not for the number.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Reduce ω¹⁰ and ω¹¹
steps.margin_note: First mark. ω³ = 1, so ω¹⁰ = (ω³)³ · ω = ω and ω¹¹ = (ω³)³ · ω² = ω². The four brackets are then two repeated pairs, so the product is [(2 − ω)(2 − ω²)]².
lines: ω¹⁰ = (ω³)³ · ω = ω,  ω¹¹ = (ω³)³ · ω² = ω²

recall.must_convey: That 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1 are used to reduce ω¹⁰ to ω and ω¹¹ to ω², so the product is a square.

steps.why: Every ω question is the same two facts: ω³ = 1 (so high powers of ω reduce) and 1 + ω + ω² = 0 (so any two of 1, ω, ω² can be replaced by minus the third). The reduction is the mark; the arithmetic after it is short.
common_mistakes: Writing ω¹⁰ = ω² or ω¹¹ = ω (dividing 10 and 11 by 3 wrongly).
Not noticing the product is a perfect square and multiplying four brackets.

steps.label: Evaluate the square
steps.margin_note: Second mark. (2 − ω)(2 − ω²) = 4 − 2(ω + ω²) + ω³ = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, using ω + ω² = −1 and ω³ = 1. Square it for 49.

recall.must_convey: That the reduced expression is evaluated to 49.
accept: evaluate the reduced form and get 49

steps.why: Multiplying out one pair and using ω + ω² = −1 and ω³ = 1 gives 7, so the square is 49.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the ω³ = 1 term, which gives 6² = 36.
